author.author_name: Neelima Kale, PhD, MD, MBA, FAAFP

list.listitem: All pregnant women should have a complete blood count (CBC) to assess their risk for anemia and hemoglobinopathy. C

A CBC is the initial test in any patients suspected of having thalassemia. Findings of mild anemia with low mean corpuscular volume and a normal red cell distribution width suggest thalassemia. If serum ferritin is normal, the diagnosis should be confirmed with hemoglobin electrophoresis. C
Symptoms typically begin after 6 months of age and vary in severity of the thalassemia variant. They include anemia, jaundice, growth retardation, and irritability.
Standard treatment of thalassemia major is through regular blood transfusions to correct the anemia, and iron chelation for associated iron overload. C
Luspatercept can reduce the transfusion burden given as an every 3 week SC injection. B
Deferoxamine is the recommended first-line therapy for transfusion-associated iron overload in people with thalassemia major.A

Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is considered the curative treatment, and should be offered to young patients with thalassemia major with an available human leukocyte antigen (HLA) identical sibling as soon as possible, ideally before iron overload and iron-related tissue damages occur. Gene therapy is also being investigated.B

background.definition: Thalassemias are a hereditary group of disorders arising from ineffective erythropoiesis due to a defect in the gene controlling the synthesis of the globin chains that make up the hemoglobin molecule.

list.listitem: Annually, an estimated 56,000 infants are born worldwide with a major thalassemia.
Globally 20% of the world’s population has at least a single gene deletion for α thalassemia.

Prevalence of α thalassemia carrier status by geographic region: Africa: 10% to 20% Middle East and India: 40% Papua New Guinea and Northern India: 80% Prevalence of β thalassemia carrier status is much less common, ranging from 1% to 20% in Africa, the Middle East, India, and South-East Asia.

Prevalence of thalassemia in the United States is unknown. Most studies are from California, where 26% of the population is foreign born and over 50% of the population is from groups associated with risk for thalassemia.
In one study, 31% of US-dwelling African-American adults had a gene deletion for α thalassemia.
Thalassemia is the most common inherited single-gene disorder in the world.
It is the most common non-sickle hemoglobinopathy in California, and hemoglobin H disease (HbH) represents over 80% of these cases.
Worldwide, 5500 perinatal deaths annually are due to α thalassemia major.
Thalassemia is caused by a defect in the synthesis of globin chains, with an excess of the present globin leading to ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis.

Normal hemoglobin chains consist of a heme molecule interlocking with one pair of α and one pair of either γ, β, or δ globin chains resulting in fetal hemoglobin (HbF), adult hemoglobin (HbA), or hemoglobin A2 (HbA2), respectively.

α globin synthesis: The two genes encoding synthesis of α globin chains are located on each chromosome 16. Deletion of one or more of the genes, represented by a minus sign, results in a deficit of the α globin chain and an excess of the β, δ, or γ globin chain: 0 gene deletions: αα/αα 1 gene deletion: αα/α- (α thalassemia silent carrier) 2 gene deletions: May occur as cis or trans deletions: 1) αα/-- (α thalassemia minor, which is more severe and more common in Asians) or 2) α-/α- (α thalassemia minor, which is less severe and more common in African-Americans) 3 gene deletions or mutations: α-/-- (HbH), ααT/-- (Hemoglobin Constant Spring, which is more common in Southeast Asians) 4 gene deletions: --/-- (Hemoglobin Bart’s; γ4 tetramer)

β globin synthesis: Genes for β globin synthesis are encoded on one gene located on chromosome 11. β thalassemias mostly occur due to mutations and, rarely, deletion of this gene resulting in decreased β globin chains. Note that “β” indicates normal synthesis, “+” indicates reduced synthesis, and “0” no synthesis of the β globin chains: 1 gene defect: β/β0 (β thalassemia minor), β/β+ (β thalassemia trait) --> seldom to occasional transfusion 2 gene defects: β0/β+, β+/β+ (β thalassemia intermedia) --> occasional to frequent transfusion 2 gene defects: β0/β0 (β thalassemia major; Cooley’s anemia) --> transfusion dependent
The USPSTF does not make any recommendations regarding screening for thalassemias. C

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends offering hemoglobinopathy screening to all pregnant women. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is recommended as part of screening to couples of African, Southeast Asian, and Mediterranean descent. If both parents are found to be carriers, genetic counseling should be offered. C
Prenatal screening is offered routinely to pregnant women in most countries, including the United States. ACOG recommends this for all pregnant women.
Premarital screening has been implemented in world regions with a high incidence of hemoglobinopathies. The goal is to identify carrier couples at risk for producing an affected child.
Preconception screening is first line in countries with lower prevalence. The mother is first screened and if found to be a carrier, then the father is tested.

There is a wide variability in state-based requirements for screening and follow-up of α thalassemia trait and silent carrier state. An inventory review of department of health websites from each of the 50 states was carried out on posted guidelines of the management of children with α thalassemia silent carrier and trait. Alpha thalassemia is not reported in 7 states, 12 states recommend reporting but have no follow-up recommendations, and 31 states have management recommendations.

Newborn screening has been recommended in several countries. Within the United States, several states have implemented newborn screening for thalassemia; however, this is not sensitive enough for thalassemia carrier detection, since HbA2 levels are not always detectable at birth.
The American College of Medical Genetics recommends including screening for hemoglobin variants in the panel for newborn screen testing across all states.

Blood transfusions may be indicated in patients with non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT) to manage or prevent extramedullary hematopoietic pseudo tumors, thrombotic disease, or heart failure, secondary to pulmonary hypertension. They may also be provided in anticipation of acute stress or blood loss, such as during surgery or pregnancy.

The CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends all post-splenectomy patients should receive haemophilus influenza, meningococcal, and the pneumococcal 23 valent polysaccharide (PPSV23) vaccines prior to surgery. The PPSV23 vaccine should be repeated 3 to 5 years later. They should also receive influenza vaccination annually.
Thalassemia is often discovered on newborn screening tests, or found incidentally, when a complete blood count (CBC) shows low mean corpuscular volume (MCV). C

A CBC is the initial test in any patients suspected of having thalassemia. Findings of mild anemia with low mean corpuscular volume and a normal red cell distribution width suggest thalassemia. If serum ferritin is normal, the diagnosis should be confirmed with hemoglobin electrophoresis. C

Hemoglobin electrophoresis cannot detect α thalassemia trait or silent carrier status in newborns. Hemoglobin electrophoresis also cannot detect HbH disease in adults as all hemoglobin molecules are missing 3 out of 4 α chains. Since all hemoglobin chains use α, the decrease is equal across the entire hemoglobin electrophoresis and thus not obvious. C

DNA analysis is the best test for detecting α thalassemia trait or silent carrier, or confirming thalassemia when there is a high clinical suspicion. As a general rule, a patient with microcytic anemia but with a normal RBC count and hemoglobin electrophoresis, who is not iron deficient, is assumed to have α thalassemia; if asymptomatic, no further testing is likely needed. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Clinical findings: Mild to moderate anemia, reticulocytosis. Peripheral smear: Adults: Sickle cells, Howell-Jolly bodies. HPLC/electrophoresis findings: Sickle cell disease, sickle cell-beta0 thalassemia, HbSD: HbS, HbA2, and HbF present; HbA absent. (DNA analysis is required for identification of these variants). Sickle cell trait: HbF, HbA, and HbS with HbA being predominant. If HbS is predominant a presumptive diagnosis of sickle cell-beta+ thalassemia is made (DNA analysis is required for confirmation in newborns)

Clinical findings: Mild to moderate anemia. Peripheral smear: Target cells, crystals, and microspherocytes. HPLC/electrophoresis findings: Hemoglobin C trait: HbA, HbC. Hemoglobin C disease: HbC, no HbA. Hemoglobin C - sickle cell: HbS, HbC; no HbA. (DNA analysis shows β globin chain mutation)

Clinical findings: None for trait and mild anemia with homozygous disease (very rare); severe anemia if sickle trait is present. HPLC/electrophoresis findings: For Hemoglobin D trait: HbA, HbD. For Hemoglobin D - sickle: HbS, HbD (DNA analysis shows β globin mutation)

Clinical findings: Hypochromia and microcytosis. Anemia with homozygous disease. HPLC/electrophoresis findings: For Hemoglobin E trait: HbE, HbA, and HbF. For Hemoglobin E disease: HbE, no HbA present

Clinical findings: Variable levels of anemia, normal to low reticulocytosis. Peripheral blood smear: Target cells, anisocytosis. HPLC/electrophoresis findings: Usually non-contributory, HbA, HbA2. Bone marrow biopsy: Bone marrow aspiration is definitive demonstrating presence of ringed sideroblasts (erythroblasts with iron containing granules surrounding the nucleus)

Clinical findings: Variable levels of hemolytic anemia, low reticulocytosis. Peripheral blood smear: Anisopoikilocytosis, few mature erythroblasts. Bone marrow biopsy: Bone marrow aspiration demonstrates abnormalities in nucleus of bone marrow red cell precursors. Genetic testing is required for confirmation

Clinical findings: Moderate anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated white blood cell count with predominantly monocytosis. Peripheral blood smear: Erythroblasts, nucleated RBC, and circulating immature myeloid cells. HPLC/electrophoresis findings: Elevated HbF levels may be detected. Bone marrow biopsy: Molecular analysis of blood or bone marrow will show acquired or inherited cell mutations

Clinical findings: Pancytopenia with decreased reticulocytosis. Peripheral blood smear: Normocytic or macrocytic cells and typically cell morphology are normally excepted if there is a coexisting hematologic disorder. Bone marrow biopsy: Bone marrow aspiration is diagnostic, demonstrating hypo cellularity and fatty infiltration of bone marrow space

list.listitem: See for diagnostic criteria for α and β thalassemias.
Of the α thalassemias, patients who are silent carriers or carry the trait are asymptomatic, and those with Hemoglobin Constant Spring are asymptomatic or only mildly symptomatic.

Patients with α thalassemia intermedia (hemoglobin H disease) have a variable clinical presentation with moderate to severe symptoms. Most affected individuals present with a microcytic, hypochromic, hemolytic anemia. More severe manifestations include splenic enlargement, and facial bone changes such as maxillary hypertrophy and frontal bossing.

Alpha thalassemia major (Hemoglobin Bart’s syndrome) is the most clinically profound presentation of α thalassemia. These fetuses present with signs of congestive heart failure in utero and are often delivered stillborn between 30 to 40 weeks’ gestation.
Beta thalassemia trait does not cause symptoms.
In older children, suspect β thalassemia intermedia if patient presents with mild anemia and hepatosplenomegaly.

Beta thalassemia major should be suspected in a child under 2 years of age if they present with progressive pallor, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, mild jaundice, and severe microcytic anemia. It takes approximately 6 months to present clinically as HbF will maintain normal oxygen exchange until its levels naturally decrease at around 6 months. Patients with persistent HbF will often fare much better.
Extramedullary hematopoiesis can cause complications such as osteoporosis, bone deformities, and facial changes, and can also affect the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.

Newborn screening: HbH disease should be suspected when a newborn screen shows >15% Hemoglobin Bart’s. On a newborn screen, β thalassemia major presents with complete absence of hemoglobin A. However, β thalassemia intermedia is difficult to detect and will need molecular genetic testing for confirmation.
A CBC showing microcytic anemia (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg) with a normal red cell distribution width (RDW) is suggestive of thalassemia and warrants further evaluation for confirmation.
Serum ferritin should be checked and, if normal, proceed to hemoglobin electrophoresis. If low, oral iron supplementation should be recommended for 3 months prior to hemoglobin electrophoresis.
See for a suggested approach for anemia and microcytosis.
Treatment of thalassemia major involves lifelong transfusions and chelation therapy to avoid iron overload.C
Some patients with HbH disease may be transfusion-dependent and will require monitoring and therapy for iron overload. C
Deferoxamine is the recommended first-line therapy for transfusion-associated iron overload in people with thalassemia major.A
Treatment of thalassemia intermedia is symptom-directed, with splenectomy and sporadic transfusions, if indicated. C
Luspatercept can reduce the transfusion burden given as an every 3 week SC injection. B

Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is considered the curative treatment and should be offered to young patients with thalassemia major with an available human leukocyte antigen (HLA) identical sibling as soon as possible, ideally before iron overload and iron-related tissue damages occur. Gene therapy is also being investigated.B

A study randomized 336 patients with transfusion dependent beta-thalassemia to luspatercept or placebo in a 2:1 ratio. The drug binds to transofmring growth factor beta ligands and enhances red cell maturation. The reduction in the transfusion burden (number of red cell units transufsed) was significantly reduced during over a week of follow-up. The reduction was at least 50% in 40% receiving luspatercept compared with 6% receiving placebo (p < 0.05, NNT = 3). Adverse events included arthralgias and bone pain, dizziness, hypertension, and hyuperuricemia. The drug is given as a 1 mg/kg injection subcutaneously every 3 weeks.

Exagamglogene autotemcel is a CRISPR-based nonviral cellular therapy that increases fetal hemoglobin production. In a case series, 32 of 35 treated patients remained transfusion independent following therapy for a median of 20 weeks.
Transfusion-dependent individuals must be monitored for iron overload and chelation therapy used as appropriate.

Three iron chelators are currently available: deferoxamine, deferiprone, and deferasirox. Deferoxamine is the recommended first-line therapy for transfusion-associated iron overload (serum ferritin >= 1000 ng/ml) in people with thalassemia major. Deferasirox represents an option for patients with contraindication, poor tolerance, or non-adherence to deferoxamine. A Cochrane review of 16 studies with 1807 patients concluded that deferasirox is not superior to deferoxamine or deferiprone at the recommended dose.

A small RCT found that amlodipine 5 mg once daily reduces myocardial iron deposition in patients undergoing chelation therapy. However, the clinical implications are unclear, and the finding requires confirmation.

A Cochrane Review of randomized trials concludes that in patients with non-transfusion-dependent β thalassemia, the administration of 10 mg/kg/day of hydroxyurea compared to 20 mg/kg/day resulted in higher hemoglobin levels and appeared safer with few adverse effects; the mean difference was -2.4 g/dL (95% CI -2.8 to -2.0). However, this intervention did not have any effect on the need for blood transfusion and was based on small RCTs. Larger trials are needed.
A phase 2 study found that the oral pyruvate kinase inhibitor mitapivat increased hemoglobin production in patients with non-transfusion dependent thalassemia.

Splenectomy may be indicated in patients with symptomatic splenomegaly or massive splenomegaly with concern for possible rupture, cytopenia secondary to hypersplenism, or when transfusion needs exceed iron chelation therapy.
Following splenectomy, patients with thalassemia major or intermedia are more likely to develop a chronic hypercoagulable state.

Patients with splenectomy are also at higher risk of infections and should be placed on prophylactic antibiotic therapy with penicillin for at least 2 years after splenectomy. Erythromycin, amoxicillin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is options for penicillin-allergic patients.

Blood transfusions remain the mainstay of therapy for β thalassemia major and the severe forms of β thalassemia intermedia and HbH. Some variants of β thalassemia intermedia and HbH disease may not always require chronic transfusion therapy. Similarly, patients with beta thalassemia trait and α thalassemia silent carriers do not require transfusions.

The hemoglobin threshold for transfusion is variable, and should not always be an indicator for transfusion in patients with NTDT, except where they have severe anemia (<5 g/dL) or to prevent other complications.Generally, a hemoglobin less than 7 g/dL appears to be widely accepted as a threshold for transfusion based on expert opinion. Facial changes, poor growth, spontaneous fractures, and other signs of extramedullary hematopoiesis are also indicators for transfusion regardless of the hemoglobin level. The target hemoglobin after transfusion is 9 g/dL to 10.5 g/dL (11 - 12 g/dl for patients with heart disease).

Extended red-blood cell phenotyping and matching of donor blood is recommended to prevent alloimmunization in transfusion-dependent patients. Based on a systematic review, a guideline recommends ABO D CcEe K-matched RBCs for patients with β-thalassemia, even in the absence of alloantibodies, to reduce the risk of alloimmunization.
There are no randomized controlled trials on the efficacy and safety of different types of allogeneic HSCT in people with severe transfusion-dependent β thalassemia major or its variants.

Non-randomized data report high cure rates and good long-term prognosis with allogenic stem cell transplant; as such, expert panels recommend this treatment option as soon as possible, ideally before occurrence of iron overload or organ damage.

A prospective cohort identified 23 transfusion dependent patients 12 years and older with β-thalassemia. They were given betibeglogene autotemcel (beti-cel) gene therapy, and at 12 months 90% were transfusion independent with a mean adult hemoglobin (HbA) level of 8.7 gm/dl and a range of 5.2 to 10.6 gm/dl.
Transfusions are lifelong for patients with β thalassemia major.

When diagnosis of thalassemia major or intermedia is made, patients will need to be under the care of a hematologist as they will require regular comprehensive visits and monitoring to be assessed for treatment and prevention of common and major complications of the disease. They can be followed by their primary care physician once a plan of care has been established.
Pain management referral may be required in patients with chronic bone pain due to bone marrow space expansion from ineffective erythropoiesis.
Cardiopulmonary complications such as acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary hypertension may occur emergently and will require hospitalization with early specialist involvement.

Chronic complications are related to ineffective erythropoiesis and iron overload and include cardiac dysfunction, disturbances of growth and sexual maturation, skeletal abnormalities, endocrine disorders, liver fibrosis, and cirrhosis.
Bisphosphonates and zinc supplementation may be used for patients with osteoporosis associated with thalassemia major.

Phosphodiesterase inhibitors have been used for treatment of pulmonary hypertension in patients with thalassemia, based on clinical trials and small studies that have demonstrated their efficacy in improving pulmonary hemodynamics and clinical symptoms.
Small case series report treatment with hydroxyurea, transfusion, and chelation having some benefit in management of leg ulcers associated with thalassemia.

A combination of high-dose IV deferoxamine augmented with oral deferiprone is recommended for the management of acute heart failure secondary to cardiac toxicity from iron overload in patients with β thalassemia major.

Open-label multicenter randomized trials have suggested that oral deferiprone is more efficacious than oral deferasirox or subcutaneous deferoxamine in reducing myocardial iron load and preserving systolic ventricular function.

Individuals with β thalassemia trait, α thalassemia trait, and α thalassemia silent carrier status usually present with a mild, microcytic anemia and do not require transfusions. These individuals should not take iron supplements unless they have a coexisting iron deficiency.

Thalassemia intermedia and HbH disease have variable clinical presentation with most patients requiring transfusions sporadically, mainly during major illnesses such as acute infections, pregnancies, or to treat symptomatic anemia that is impairing childhood development. Collectively, these thalassemias are referred to as non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT).

There is no specific hemoglobin level in NTDT that dictates the need for transfusion. Transfusion therapy is used in cases of severe growth restriction, splenic enlargement, leg ulcers, thrombosis, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, and acute infections causing anemia.
NTDT patients are at increased risk of thromboembolic events; this risk is increased after splenectomy but greatly reduced by transfusions.
The most common complications noted in NTDT are osteoporosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, hypogonadism, cholelithiasis, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension, abnormal liver function, and leg ulcers.
Consider iron chelation with deferoxamine if serum ferritin is >= 800 ng/ml in NTDT patients.

Patients with β thalassemia major require lifelong transfusions to maintain normal growth and Hb levels >9.5 g/dL. Transfusion therapy is usually initiated at hemoglobin levels <7.0 gm/dL or if there is evidence of poor growth, facial changes, fractures, or clinically relevant extramedullary hematopoiesis, irrespective of hemoglobin level.
Iron chelation should be considered if serum ferritin >= 1000 ng/ml with deferoxamine as first line therapy.
Allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is considered curative.
Leukoreduced red cells with extended phenotype and antigen matching for C, c, D, E, e, Kell, and Duffy antigens are recommended for transfusion to prevent transfusion reactions and alloimmunization.

Transfusion-dependent individuals are at risk of iron overload and need regular monitoring of iron load (serum ferritin every 1 to 3 months, liver iron concentration by MRI every 6 months to 24 months).
Monitoring is also required for anemia and its complications, endocrine function, and nutritional deficiencies.

Hemoglobin Bart’s hydrops fetalis syndrome (BHFS) is usually fatal. An international registry of survivors report intrauterine therapy with intrauterine transfusions or hematopoietic stem cell transfusions may provide short-term benefits. In one study, 20% (n=55) of BHFS survivors suffered from a severe neurodevelopmental delay of at least 6 months. There are associated congenital abnormalities and these patients require lifelong transfusions.
Thalassemia minor trait: Prognosis of thalassemia minor trait patients is excellent.B
Thalassemia intermedia: Prognosis in these patients is often dictated by their need for transfusion and subsequent iron overload.B

Beta thalassemia major: This condition was fatal by age 5 before the advent of therapy. However, this has improved over the past 20 years due to advances in transfusion therapy and treatments for iron overload.B

Homozygous α thalassemia is presumed to be uniformly fatal in the intrauterine period; however, early prenatal diagnosis, intrauterine transfusions, and hematopoietic stem cell transplants have the potential to improve survival and prognosis.B
Recommended monthly assessment for patients with thalassemia major: CBC, serum ferritin, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis. C

Annual assessment: Hearing and vision screening; cardiac MRI starting at age 10; hepatic iron measurement and bone mineral density; age-based annual laboratory screens for bone health and endocrine function including TSH and free T4, fasting glucose, parathyroid hormone, ionized calcium, and gonadotropins (LH, FSH, estradiol, and testosterone); and screening for nutritional deficiencies (Vitamin D and trace elements).C

Preconception counseling for women with thalassemia should include genetic testing of the partner, iron burden, liver and cardiac function, glucose tolerance, assessment of risk of infection and thrombosis, and extensive phenotype and genotype screening in preparation for transfusion.
Women with thalassemia need increased folic acid supplementation during pregnancy.
Women with β thalassemia minor, α thalassemia trait, and HbH have favorable pregnancy outcomes.

Population-based studies investigating outcomes in women with β thalassemia minor report higher rates of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) (OR 2.4; 95% CI 1.4% - 4.2%), and oligohydramnios (OR 2.1; 95% CI 1.2% - 3.7%), compared to all pregnancies, but no differences in perinatal outcomes.
Pregnancy in women with β thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent thalassemia is recommended only if cardiac function is normal and the overall burden due to iron overload is low.
These pregnancies are considered high risk and need monitoring of maternal iron load, liver functions, and cardiac function in addition to increased fetal monitoring for growth restriction.
Target hemoglobin for women with transfusion-dependent thalassemia is 10 mg/dL to support adequate fetal oxygenation.
Clinical data on iron chelation therapy during pregnancy are lacking and current recommendations advise against use of iron chelators during pregnancy.
Prophylactic anticoagulation may be needed in women with transfusion-dependent thalassemia.
Hypogonadism and ovulation abnormalities are present in 30% to 80% of adult women with transfusion-dependent thalassemia.
Younger thalassemia patients often have indwelling vascular access devices and are at risk for central line-associated bloodstream infections and thromboembolism.
Children under age 5 carry the greatest risk for severe infections with encapsulated bacteria and as such, splenectomy is not recommended routinely.
Immunization against pneumococcal infections, meningococcal infections, and H influenzae type B should be performed before elective splenectomy or as soon as possible after emergent splenectomy.
Following splenectomy, children under age 2 should be on oral penicillin 125 mg twice daily until age 2, then 250 mg twice daily until at least 5 years of age.

feature.caption: Thalassemias, their diagnostic criteria, and their prognosis.
feature.feature_body:
Hematology, electrophoresis, and HPLC findings Prognosis
Alpha thalassemias
Alpha thalassemia major (Hb Bart’s disease) Severe, usually fatal microcytic hypochromic anemia Hb Bart’s disease is usually fatal in utero without early intrauterine interventions such as transfusions.
HbA, HbA2, and HbF usually absent
Hb Bart’s (γ4 globin chain) present
Alpha thalassemia intermedia (HbH or HbH-CS** Moderate to severe microcytic hypochromic anemia Varied prognosis dependent on transfusion requirements and risk for iron overload.
HbA2 <4%
HbF <1%
HbH (β globin chain) increased ± HbCS
Alpha thalassemia trait** Microcytosis and hypochromia Excellent
HbA2 <4%
HbF <1%
(Normal electrophoresis)
Alpha thalassemia silent carrier** Normal RBC or mild microcytosis Excellent
HbA2 <4%
HbF <1%
(Normal electrophoresis)
Beta thalassemias
Beta thalassemia major Severe microcytic/normocytic anemia Poor prognosis as lifelong transfusions are needed and patients are at high risk for iron overload. Childhood HSCT is considered curative and improves prognosis.
HbA absent
HbA2 increased (>5%, up to 95%) on electrophoresis*
HbF increased in some variants
Beta thalassemia intermedia** Moderate microcytic hypochromic anemia Varied prognosis, dependent on transfusion requirements and risk for iron overload
HbA2 Increased (>4%)
HbF increased (>5% to 50%)
Beta thalassemia trait or beta thalassemia minor** Microcytosis and hypochromia with or without anemia Excellent
HbA2 increased ≥4%
HbF 0.1% to 5%
*This A band is further analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), which can delineate true HbA (α/δ) from Hb C, E, or O, which also run at the A band on gel electrophoresis. **Confirmed through DNA analysis for α and β globin mutations HSCT: hematopoietic stem cell transplant Reference:
